items.title: Ecosystem, Energy Flow & Ecological Pyramids
items.body:
### Ecosystem, energy flow and ecological pyramids

**In one line**
An ecosystem is living things plus their surroundings working as one unit, and energy moves through it in only one direction, shrinking at every step.

**Why it is asked**
The 10% law, the "which pyramid can invert" question, and grazing-vs-detritus food chains are repeat favourites.

**The story**
An **ecosystem** is a working unit where **biotic** parts (living: producers, consumers, decomposers) interact with **abiotic** parts (non-living: light, water, soil, temperature). **Producers** (green plants) capture sunlight; **consumers** eat others — primary (herbivores), then secondary and tertiary; **decomposers** break down the dead and recycle nutrients. Energy passes along a **food chain** through steps called **trophic levels**, and many chains linked together form a more stable **food web**. The crucial rule is **Lindeman's 10% law**: only about **10% of the energy at one level reaches the next** — the rest is lost as heat and in respiration. Because so much is lost, chains rarely run beyond **4-5 links**. This loss also shapes **ecological pyramids**: the **pyramid of energy is always upright** (energy only shrinks upward), while pyramids of **number** and **biomass can sometimes be inverted** (for example, one big tree feeding many insects, or few large fish supported by vast tiny plankton in a pond).

**Picture it**

| Pyramid | Usually | Can it invert? |
|---|---|---|
| Number | Upright | Yes (a tree, or parasites) |
| Biomass | Upright | Yes (aquatic/pond) |
| Energy | Upright | Never (10% law) |

**Terms explained**
- **Biotic / abiotic** = living parts / non-living parts of an ecosystem.
- **Trophic level** = a feeding step (producer, herbivore, carnivore).
- **Grazing food chain** = starts with living green plants.
- **Detritus food chain** = starts with dead organic matter.

**Don't confuse**
- **Only the energy pyramid can never invert.** Number and biomass pyramids can.
- Energy flow is **one-way (unidirectional)**; it does not cycle back like nutrients do.

**Remember it**
"Energy only falls, and only 10% survives each step — so the energy pyramid stands tall."

**TL;DR**
- Ecosystem = biotic + abiotic parts interacting as one unit.
- Energy flow is one-way; the 10% law passes only ~10% upward.
- Grazing chain starts with green plants; detritus chain with dead matter.
- Pyramid of energy is always upright; number and biomass pyramids can invert.
keyPoints: Ecosystem = biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) + abiotic components interacting as a functional unit.
Energy flow is unidirectional; Lindeman's 10% law passes only ~10% of energy to the next trophic level.
Grazing food chain starts with green plants; detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter.
Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright; pyramids of number and biomass can be inverted.
Food chains rarely exceed 4-5 trophic links because of energy loss.

items.title: Biodiversity, Hotspots & India's Megadiversity
items.body:
### Biodiversity, hotspots and India's megadiversity

**In one line**
Biodiversity is the variety of life at three levels, and a "hotspot" is a region that is both exceptionally rich and badly threatened — India has four.

**Why it is asked**
The three levels, the "17 megadiverse / ~2.4% land, ~8% species" statistic, and the two-part hotspot definition are standard statement-based facts.

**The story**
**Biodiversity** comes in three levels: **genetic** (variety within a species), **species** (variety of different species), and **ecosystem** (variety of habitats). India is **one of 17 megadiverse countries** — with only about **2.4% of the world's land area** it holds roughly **8% of all recorded global biodiversity**. Some regions matter more than others. A **biodiversity hotspot**, as defined by Norman Myers, must pass **two tests together**: it must have at least **1,500 endemic (found-nowhere-else) vascular plant species**, AND it must have already **lost at least 70% of its original (primary) vegetation** — so it is both rich and under threat. **Four hotspots reach into India**: the **Himalaya**, the **Western Ghats and Sri Lanka**, **Indo-Burma** (covering the North-East), and **Sundaland** (the Nicobar Islands).

**Picture it**

| Hotspot | Coverage in India |
|---|---|
| Himalaya | The Indian Himalayan region |
| Western Ghats & Sri Lanka | Western coastal ranges |
| Indo-Burma | North-East India (excluding the Ghats) |
| Sundaland | Nicobar Islands |

**Terms explained**
- **Endemic** = found naturally in one place and nowhere else.
- **Vascular plant** = a plant with water-conducting tissue (most land plants).
- **Megadiverse country** = one of 17 nations holding most of Earth's species.
- **Primary vegetation** = the original, undisturbed natural plant cover.

**Don't confuse**
- A hotspot needs **both** conditions (endemism AND 70% habitat loss), not either one alone.
- "Megadiverse" (a country) is not the same as a "hotspot" (a region).
- Not every famous hotspot touches India: the **Cerrado** (a tropical savanna in **Brazil**), Madagascar and the Atlantic Forest are hotspots **outside India**. India's four are only Himalaya, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Sundaland.

**Remember it**
"Hotspot = Rich (1,500 endemic plants) + Robbed (70% lost)." India has four.

**TL;DR**
- Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species, ecosystem.
- India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; ~2.4% land holds ~8% of global biodiversity.
- Hotspot (Myers) = ≥1,500 endemic plants AND ≥70% primary vegetation lost.
- Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Sundaland (Nicobar).
keyPoints: Three levels of biodiversity: genetic, species and ecosystem.
India is one of 17 megadiverse countries; ~2.4% land area holds ~8% of global recorded biodiversity.
A biodiversity hotspot needs >=1,500 endemic plant species AND >=70% loss of primary vegetation (Myers).
Four hotspots touch India: Himalaya, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (Nicobar).
Western Ghats and North-East (Indo-Burma) are the most biodiverse Indian regions.
Cerrado (Brazilian savanna) is a hotspot that does NOT extend into India.

items.title: Environmental Legal Framework of India
items.body:
### India's environmental legal framework

**In one line**
A stack of laws protects India's environment, with the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 as the "umbrella" over all of them.

**Why it is asked**
Act-to-year matching, the "umbrella law" tag, and recent renames/amendments (Forest Act 2023, WPA 2022) are frequent one-markers.

**The story**
India built its environmental law piece by piece. The **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** created protected areas and species schedules — **Schedule I species enjoy the highest degree of protection** (hunting them is completely banned, e.g. tiger, Olive Ridley turtle) — and it provides for the constitution of the **National Board for Wildlife (NBWL)**, chaired by the Prime Minister, which advises on wildlife policy and clears projects in protected areas. The **Water Act, 1974** set up the **Central and State Pollution Control Boards (CPCB/SPCBs)**. The **Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980** curbed the diversion of forest land, and the **Air Act, 1981** tackled air pollution. After the **Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)**, the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** was passed as the **umbrella law** — it empowers the Centre to take *any* measure to protect the environment and is the parent of rules like the EIA (Environmental Impact Assessment) notifications; it also gives effect to the **Stockholm Conference of 1972**. Later came the **Biological Diversity Act, 2002** (creating the National Biodiversity Authority, State Boards and local committees) and the **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010** (a fast-track green court). Recent updates: the WPA was **amended in 2022** to just **four schedules**; the Forest Act was **renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam in 2023**; and the Biological Diversity Act was **amended in 2023**.

**Picture it**

| Act | Year | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Wildlife (Protection) Act | 1972 | Protected areas, species schedules |
| Water Act | 1974 | Created CPCB/SPCBs |
| Forest (Conservation) Act | 1980 | Curbs forest-land diversion |
| Air Act | 1981 | Air pollution control |
| Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | Umbrella law (post-Bhopal) |
| Biological Diversity Act | 2002 | NBA, SBBs, BMCs |
| National Green Tribunal Act | 2010 | Green court |

**Terms explained**
- **Umbrella law** = a broad parent Act under which many specific rules are issued.
- **EIA** = Environmental Impact Assessment, a study before clearing a project.
- **NBA** = National Biodiversity Authority (at Chennai).
- **NGT** = National Green Tribunal (principal bench, New Delhi).

**Don't confuse**
- The **CPCB was created by the Water Act (1974)**, not the EPA.
- The **NGT came from a separate 2010 Act**, not from the EPA 1986.

**Remember it**
"Bhopal 1984 → EPA 1986, the umbrella." Water (1974) made the pollution boards.

**TL;DR**
- EPA 1986 is the umbrella law, enacted after Bhopal (1984), giving effect to Stockholm 1972.
- Water Act (1974) created CPCB/SPCBs; Air Act 1981; NGT Act 2010.
- WPA 1972 amended in 2022 to four schedules.
- Forest Act 1980 renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam (2023); Biological Diversity Act 2002 (NBA, Chennai), amended 2023.
keyPoints: EPA 1986 is the umbrella environmental law, enacted after the 1984 Bhopal tragedy and giving effect to Stockholm 1972.
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 was amended in 2022 to just four schedules.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 was renamed Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam by the 2023 amendment.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), SBBs and BMCs; amended 2023.
Water Act (1974) created CPCB/SPCBs; NGT Act 2010 established the National Green Tribunal (principal bench, Delhi).
WPA 1972: Schedule I species enjoy the highest degree of protection; the Act provides for the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL), chaired by the PM.

items.title: Protected Areas & Wildlife Conservation
items.body:
### Protected areas and wildlife conservation

**In one line**
India protects wildlife through four kinds of protected area and a set of flagship species projects, backed by the latest forest and tiger data.

**Why it is asked**
The National-Park-vs-Sanctuary rights distinction, the species-project years, and ISFR 2023 figures are high-yield facts.

**The story**
The **Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972** sets up four protected-area types with different levels of control. A **National Park** has the **highest protection — no rights and no grazing** are allowed. A **Wildlife Sanctuary** is slightly more relaxed — certain **regulated rights** may be permitted. A **Conservation Reserve** is government land next to a park or sanctuary, managed with the community, and a **Community Reserve** is private or community land that people volunteer to conserve. India's network has grown to about **900 protected areas** — roughly **106 national parks, 573 wildlife sanctuaries, 123 conservation reserves and 86 community reserves**, covering about **5.3% of the country's area**. Flagship **species projects** anchor recovery: **Project Tiger (1973)**, now run by the **NTCA (2005)**; **Project Elephant (1992)**; and **Project Cheetah (2022)**, which brought African cheetahs to **Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh**. India has **58 tiger reserves** and a wild tiger population of **3,682 (2022 census, about 70% of the world's)**. The **India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023** records forest cover at **21.76%** and forest-plus-tree cover at **25.17%** of the geographical area, with mangroves at **4,991.68 km2** (West Bengal's Sundarbans the largest).

**Picture it**

| Project | Year | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Project Tiger | 1973 | NTCA (2005) |
| Project Elephant | 1992 | MoEFCC |
| Project Cheetah | 2022 | Kuno NP (MP) |

**Terms explained**
- **National Park** = strictest protected area; no private rights or grazing.
- **Wildlife Sanctuary** = protected area where some regulated rights may continue.
- **NTCA** = National Tiger Conservation Authority, the statutory tiger body.
- **ISFR** = India State of Forest Report, the biennial forest-cover survey by the Forest Survey of India.
- **Forest cover (ISFR definition)** = all land of **one hectare or more** with a **tree canopy density of 10% or more**, whatever its legal status or ownership (so orchards and plantations count too).

**Don't confuse**
- **National Park = no rights; Sanctuary = some regulated rights.** This is the key WPA distinction.
- **Forest cover (21.76%)** is less than **forest + tree cover (25.17%)** — quote the right one.

**Remember it**
"Park = strictest; Project Tiger 1973, NTCA 2005, Cheetah 2022 at Kuno."

**TL;DR**
- Four PA types: National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve.
- Network ~900 PAs (~106 NPs, 573 WLS) covering ~5.3% of area.
- Project Tiger 1973 (NTCA 2005), Project Elephant 1992, Project Cheetah 2022 (Kuno); 58 tiger reserves, 3,682 tigers (2022).
- ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76%, forest+tree 25.17%; mangroves 4,991.68 km2 (WB largest).
keyPoints: National Park allows no rights/grazing; a sanctuary may permit regulated rights (key WPA distinction).
Conservation reserves are govt land near PAs; community reserves are private/community conserved land.
Project Tiger began 1973; NTCA created 2005; India has 58 tiger reserves (2025) with 3,682 tigers (2022).
Project Elephant 1992; Project Cheetah 2022 reintroduced African cheetahs at Kuno NP, Madhya Pradesh.
ISFR 2023: forest cover 21.76% and forest+tree cover 25.17% of geographical area; mangroves 4,991.68 km2 (WB largest, the Sundarbans).
ISFR forest cover = all land of one hectare or more with tree canopy density of 10% or more.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Protected Areas & Wetlands
items.body:
### Andhra Pradesh — protected areas and wetlands

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh holds India's largest tiger reserve, a famous mangrove sanctuary, and a cluster of important lakes and hill forests.

**Why it is asked**
"Which is AP's only Ramsar site", "largest tiger reserve", and Coringa/Pulicat facts are repeatedly tested, singly and as match-the-list.

**The story**
Andhra Pradesh's crown jewel is the **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (NSTR)** in the **Nallamala hills** — the **largest tiger reserve in India**, shared with Telangana. Its national parks are **Papikonda** (on the Godavari, Eastern Ghats) and **Sri Venkateswara** (the Tirupati/Seshachalam hills). Along the coast, the **Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary** in the Godavari estuary near Kakinada is India's **second-largest mangrove** formation (after the Sundarbans). **Pulicat Lake**, shared with Tamil Nadu, is India's **second-largest brackish-water lagoon** (after Chilika); its AP side is the **Pulicat Lake Bird Sanctuary**, with the **Nelapattu** pelican sanctuary nearby. **Kolleru Lake**, between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, is one of India's largest freshwater lakes and **AP's only Ramsar site** (designated 2002); it was also declared a **wildlife sanctuary** (1999) for its importance as a bird habitat (grey pelicans, painted storks). **Rollapadu Wildlife Sanctuary** protects the **Great Indian Bustard**, and the **Seshachalam** hills (red-sanders forest, Tirupati region of the Eastern Ghats) form AP's **biosphere reserve (2010)**.

**Red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus)** is AP's most famous tree. It is **endemic to the Eastern Ghats of southern India** — chiefly the **Seshachalam and Nallamala hills** of Andhra Pradesh. It is listed as **Endangered on the IUCN Red List** and is **protected under CITES** (international trade controlled). Its deep-red, **high-value timber** (prized abroad for furniture and instruments) makes it a frequent **target of illegal logging and smuggling**.

**Which law or body governs each AP site**

| AP site | Governing instrument / body |
|---|---|
| Kolleru Lake | **Ramsar Convention on Wetlands** (Ramsar site) + wildlife sanctuary notified under the **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972** |
| Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve | Administered under **Project Tiger / NTCA under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972** (tiger reserves are notified under this Act) |
| Seshachalam Hills | Biosphere reserve under the **UNESCO Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme** framework (India's national biosphere-reserve scheme follows MAB) |
| Coringa | **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 — mangrove wildlife sanctuary** |

**Don't confuse:** Seshachalam is a biosphere reserve under India's MAB-based scheme but is **not** one of India's 12 sites on UNESCO's World Network; Kolleru is the **Ramsar** site, Coringa is a **WPA sanctuary**, not a Ramsar site.

**Picture it**

| Area | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam | Tiger Reserve | Largest in India (Nallamala) |
| Coringa | Wildlife Sanctuary | 2nd-largest mangrove in India; Godavari estuary near Kakinada |
| Pulicat | Lagoon/bird sanctuary | 2nd-largest brackish lagoon; shared with Tamil Nadu |
| Kolleru | Freshwater lake | AP's only Ramsar site (2002) |
| Seshachalam | Biosphere reserve | Red-sanders forest (2010) |

**Terms explained**
- **Brackish water** = water saltier than fresh but less salty than the sea.
- **Estuary** = where a river's mouth meets the sea, mixing fresh and salt water.
- **Ramsar site** = a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention.
- **Mangrove** = salt-tolerant coastal forest that shields the shore.

**Don't confuse**
- **Kolleru (freshwater) is AP's Ramsar site; Pulicat is a brackish lagoon**, not the Ramsar site.
- **Coringa = 2nd-largest mangrove; Pulicat = 2nd-largest brackish lagoon** — different "second-largest" titles.

**Remember it**
"NSTR biggest tiger, Coringa the mangrove, Kolleru the Ramsar lake, Seshachalam the biosphere."

**TL;DR**
- Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam = India's largest tiger reserve (Nallamala, shared with Telangana).
- Coringa = India's 2nd-largest mangrove; Pulicat = 2nd-largest brackish lagoon.
- Kolleru = AP's only Ramsar site (2002); Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
- Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; Rollapadu protects the Great Indian Bustard.

**Latest Ramsar additions (keep current):** Surha Tal/Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary, Ballia (UP) — 100th, 5 Jun 2026; **Glaw Lake**, Lohit (Arunachal Pradesh) — 101st, 3 Aug 2026; **Sukhna Wetland**, Chandigarh (Chandigarh’s first) and **Sauj Jheel**, Mainpuri (UP) — announced 15 Oct 2026, taking India to **103**. Mainpuri is the only district with two Ramsar sites (Saman and Sauj Jheel).
keyPoints: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve is the LARGEST tiger reserve in India (Nallamala hills), shared with Telangana.
Coringa WLS (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove formation after the Sundarbans.
Pulicat Lake is India's second-largest brackish-water lagoon (after Chilika), on the AP-Tamil Nadu border.
Kolleru Lake is AP's only Ramsar site (designated 2002); Papikonda and Sri Venkateswara are AP national parks.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; Rollapadu WLS protects the Great Indian Bustard.
Red sanders: endemic to the southern Eastern Ghats (Seshachalam-Nallamala, AP); IUCN Endangered; CITES-protected; target of illegal logging and smuggling.
Governance links: Kolleru = Ramsar + WPA sanctuary; NSTR = Project Tiger/NTCA under WPA 1972; Seshachalam = UNESCO MAB framework; Coringa = WPA mangrove sanctuary.
India has 103 Ramsar sites (Sukhna, Chandigarh and Sauj Jheel, UP added 15 Oct 2026).

items.title: Wetlands, Biosphere Reserves & Species Conventions
items.body:
### Wetlands, biosphere reserves and species conventions

**In one line**
A set of global agreements protects wetlands (Ramsar), model ecosystems (UNESCO biosphere reserves) and threatened or traded species (CITES, CMS, CBD).

**Why it is asked**
Ramsar's year/place, India's site count and "most in Tamil Nadu", the first biosphere reserve, and convention-to-focus matching are reliable facts.

**The story**
The **Ramsar Convention on Wetlands** was signed in **1971 at Ramsar, Iran**, to conserve wetlands and promote their **"wise use"**. **India joined in 1982** and now has **103 Ramsar sites (as of October 2026)** — the **most are in Tamil Nadu**. The **Montreux Record** is a watch-list of Ramsar sites facing harmful ecological change (India's are **Keoladeo** and **Loktak**). Separately, **biosphere reserves** are designated under **UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme (1971)** and zoned into **core, buffer and transition** areas; India has **18 biosphere reserves**, of which **Nilgiri (1986)** was the first and **12** are on the UNESCO **World Network (WNBR)** — AP's is **Seshachalam (2010)**. For species, four instruments recur: the **IUCN Red List** rates conservation status; **CITES (1973)** controls trade in endangered species; **CMS/Bonn (1979)** protects migratory species (India hosted **COP13 at Gandhinagar in 2020**); and the **CBD (Rio, 1992)** covers biodiversity, with its **Cartagena** (biosafety) and **Nagoya** (benefit-sharing) protocols.

**How the lists apply to one species — the Olive Ridley sea turtle.** It is classified **Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List**, is listed in **Appendix I of CITES** (no commercial trade) and in **Schedule I of India's Wildlife (Protection) Act** (highest protection). It is famous for **'arribada'** (Spanish for "arrival") — **synchronised mass nesting**, when thousands of females come ashore together; India's big arribada beaches are in Odisha (Gahirmatha, Rushikulya), and it also nests along the Andhra Pradesh coast.

**Picture it**

| Body | Focus |
|---|---|
| IUCN Red List | Conservation status (CR/EN/VU...) |
| CITES (1973) | Trade in endangered species |
| CMS / Bonn (1979) | Migratory species |
| CBD (1992) | Biodiversity; Cartagena & Nagoya protocols |

**Terms explained**
- **Wise use** = sustainable use of wetlands without destroying them.
- **Montreux Record** = Ramsar's list of threatened wetland sites.
- **MAB zones** = core (strictly protected), buffer, transition (human activity allowed).
- **CITES Appendices** = lists I-III ranking trade restrictions by threat level.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ramsar (wetlands) is NOT a UNESCO body** — biosphere reserves are the UNESCO (MAB) ones.
- **CITES = trade; CMS = migration; IUCN Red List = status; CBD = diversity.**

**Remember it**
"Ramsar 1971 Iran; Nilgiri 1986 first biosphere; CITES trades, CMS migrates."

**TL;DR**
- Ramsar Convention signed 1971 (Ramsar, Iran); India joined 1982, has 101 sites (2026), most in Tamil Nadu.
- Montreux Record flags threatened sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
- Biosphere reserves under UNESCO MAB (1971): India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first, 12 on WNBR; Seshachalam (2010) in AP.
- CITES (1973) trade, CMS/Bonn (1979) migratory, CBD (1992) biodiversity (Cartagena, Nagoya).
keyPoints: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran; India joined in 1982 and has 101 sites (2026).
Tamil Nadu has the most Ramsar sites in India; the Montreux Record flags threatened sites (Keoladeo, Loktak).
Biosphere reserves follow UNESCO MAB (1971) with core/buffer/transition zones; India has 18, Nilgiri (1986) first.
Seshachalam (2010) is AP's biosphere reserve; 12 Indian reserves are on the UNESCO World Network (WNBR).
CITES (1973) regulates trade; CMS/Bonn (1979) covers migratory species (India hosted CMS COP13, Gandhinagar 2020); CBD (Rio 1992) has the Cartagena and Nagoya protocols.
Olive Ridley turtle: IUCN Vulnerable; CITES Appendix I; WPA Schedule I; synchronised mass nesting called 'arribada'.

items.title: Climate Change & the International Framework
items.body:
### Climate change and the international framework

**In one line**
Greenhouse gases warm the planet, the IPCC assesses the science, and a chain of treaties from the UNFCCC to the Paris Agreement coordinates the global response.

**Why it is asked**
GHG identification, IPCC parentage, the UNFCCC-Kyoto-Paris timeline, and recent-COP facts (Loss and Damage, Belem) are directly examinable.

**The story**
**Greenhouse gases (GHGs)** — carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), water vapour, ozone, CFCs and **sulphur hexafluoride (SF6, the highest global-warming potential)** — trap outgoing heat and drive **global warming**. The **IPCC**, set up jointly by the **WMO and UNEP in 1988**, *assesses* (does not conduct) climate science; its **Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2021-23)** warns warming will likely cross **1.5 degrees C** in the near term. The treaty chain begins with the **UNFCCC (Rio, 1992)**, the parent framework built on **"common but differentiated responsibilities"**. The **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** set **binding targets on developed nations** and used market mechanisms. The **Paris Agreement (2015, COP21)** asks all countries to hold warming **well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C** through self-set **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)** and net-zero goals. Recent conferences: **COP27 (2022, Sharm el-Sheikh)** created the **Loss and Damage Fund**; **COP28 (2023, Dubai)** held the first **Global Stocktake** and called to "transition away from fossil fuels"; **COP29 (2024, Baku)** set a new climate-finance goal; and **COP30 (November 2025, Belem, Brazil)** in the Amazon focused on implementation and forests.

**Picture it**

| Instrument | Year | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| UNFCCC | 1992 | Parent framework; CBDR |
| Kyoto Protocol | 1997 | Binding targets on developed nations |
| Paris Agreement | 2015 | Well below 2 C, pursue 1.5 C; NDCs |

**Terms explained**
- **GHG** = greenhouse gas, which traps heat in the atmosphere.
- **CBDR** = common but differentiated responsibilities (richer, higher-emitting nations do more).
- **NDC** = Nationally Determined Contribution, each country's self-set climate pledge.
- **Global Stocktake** = a periodic review of collective progress under Paris.

**Don't confuse**
- **The IPCC assesses science; it does not run experiments or set targets.**
- **UNFCCC (1992) is the parent; Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015)** sit under it — keep the order.

**Remember it**
"Rio 1992 (UNFCCC) → Kyoto 1997 → Paris 2015." Loss & Damage = COP27 (2022).

**TL;DR**
- Main GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs, SF6 (highest GWP).
- IPCC (WMO+UNEP, 1988); AR6 warns of crossing 1.5 C in the near term.
- UNFCCC (1992) parent; Kyoto (1997) binding on developed nations; Paris (2015) well below 2 C via NDCs.
- Loss and Damage Fund at COP27 (2022); COP28 (2023) first Global Stocktake; COP30 at Belem (Nov 2025).
keyPoints: Main GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O, water vapour, ozone, CFCs and SF6 (highest global-warming potential).
IPCC (WMO+UNEP, 1988) AR6 (2021-23) warns warming will likely cross 1.5 C in the near term.
UNFCCC (Rio 1992) is the parent treaty; Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding targets on developed nations.
Paris Agreement (2015, COP21) aims to hold warming well below 2 C (pursue 1.5 C) via nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 (2022); COP28 (2023) held the first Global Stocktake; COP30 was held at Belem, Brazil (Nov 2025).

items.title: India's Climate Action, NAPCC & Pollution Control
items.body:
### India's climate action, NAPCC and pollution control

**In one line**
India backs its net-zero-by-2070 pledge with five quantified targets (Panchamrit), eight national missions (NAPCC), a lifestyle movement (Mission LiFE) and pollution/disaster laws.

**Why it is asked**
The five Panchamrit numbers, the "eight missions" count, Mission LiFE, and the DM Act/NDMA chain are frequent single-fact and match items.

**The story**
At **COP26 (Glasgow, 2021)** India announced **Panchamrit** (five nectars): **500 GW** non-fossil capacity by 2030, **50%** of energy from renewables by 2030, cutting **1 billion tonnes** of CO2 by 2030, reducing the **emissions intensity of GDP by 45%** by 2030, and **net-zero by 2070**. The policy engine is the **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008)** with **eight missions** — Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, and Strategic Knowledge — mirrored by **State Action Plans (SAPCCs)**. India also leads a demand-side movement, **Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment, 2022)** — an India-led initiative promoting **mindful, pro-planet individual lifestyles** ("Pro Planet People"), and two India-initiated coalitions, the **International Solar Alliance (ISA)** and the **Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI)**. On pollution and disasters, the **National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019)** targets particulate cuts (tracked via the **AQI**, a six-category air-quality index); **single-use plastics were banned from 1 July 2022**; and the **Disaster Management Act, 2005** created the **NDMA — the apex disaster body, chaired by the Prime Minister**, SDMAs and the **NDRF**, with India following the global **Sendai Framework (2015-30)** — vital for AP's cyclone-prone coast.

**Picture it**

| Panchamrit target (by 2030) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Non-fossil capacity | 500 GW |
| Energy from renewables | 50% |
| CO2 reduction | 1 billion tonnes |
| Emissions intensity of GDP | down 45% |
| Net-zero | by 2070 |

**Terms explained**
- **Net-zero** = balancing emissions released with emissions removed.
- **Emissions intensity** = emissions per unit of GDP, not total emissions.
- **AQI** = Air Quality Index, with six bands from Good to Severe.
- **NDMA/NDRF** = National Disaster Management Authority / National Disaster Response Force.

**Don't confuse**
- **Net-zero is 2070, but the other four Panchamrit targets are for 2030.**
- **Mission LiFE is a behaviour movement, not a NAPCC mission.**

**Remember it**
"5 nectars: 500 GW, 50%, 1 bn t, 45% less intensity, net-zero 2070." NAPCC = 8 missions.

**TL;DR**
- Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil, 50% renewables, cut 1 bn t CO2, -45% emissions intensity (all 2030), net-zero 2070.
- NAPCC (2008) has eight missions; states have SAPCCs.
- Mission LiFE (2022) is India's pro-planet lifestyle push; ISA and CDRI are India-initiated.
- NCAP (2019) + AQI; single-use plastic banned 1 July 2022; DM Act 2005 (NDMA/NDRF), Sendai 2015-30.
keyPoints: Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil by 2030, 50% renewables, cut 1 bn t CO2, -45% emissions intensity, net-zero by 2070.
NAPCC (2008) has eight missions incl. Solar, Energy Efficiency, Green India, Water and Himalayan Ecosystem; states have SAPCCs.
Mission LiFE (2022) is India's pro-planet lifestyle initiative; ISA and CDRI are India-initiated global coalitions.
National Clean Air Programme (2019) uses AQI (6 bands); single-use plastic banned from 1 July 2022.
Disaster Management Act 2005 created NDMA (chaired by PM) and NDRF; India follows the Sendai Framework 2015-30.

items.title: Pollution, Climate Concepts & Ecology — Exam Fact Cluster
items.body:
### Pollution, climate concepts and ecology — exam fact cluster

**In one line**
This note bundles the tricky one-fact items APPSC loves: geoengineering, carbon fertilization, pollution chemistry, fertiliser effects and ecology traps.

**Why it is asked**
Each cluster matches a real statement-based MCQ, where one wrong word (e.g. "nanoparticles do not exist in nature") flips the answer.

**The story**
Some ideas appear again and again. **Geoengineering / Solar Radiation Management (SRM)** — such as injecting **sulphate aerosols** into the stratosphere or **thinning cirrus clouds** — is proposed to **reduce global warming** by reflecting or releasing heat. **Carbon fertilization** means **extra plant growth caused by higher atmospheric CO2**. **Remote sensing** can measure **chlorophyll in vegetation, greenhouse-gas emissions from rice paddies, and land-surface temperature**. **Neem-coated urea** is promoted because it **slows urea's dissolution in soil**, raising nitrogen-use efficiency. In pollution chemistry, **acid rain** comes from **SO2 and NOx** forming sulphuric and nitric acid; **photochemical smog** needs **NOx + VOCs + sunlight**, producing ozone and **PAN (peroxyacetyl nitrate)**; and **eutrophication** is nutrient (N, P) over-enrichment of water. **Excess nitrogen fertiliser** raises **soil acidity** and **leaches nitrate into groundwater** (it does **not** boost nitrogen-fixing microbes). **Bisphenol A (BPA)** is a component of **polycarbonate** plastic and an **endocrine disruptor**; **benzene** is a VOC from automobile (vehicle) exhaust, tobacco smoke and wood burning. In ecology, **decomposers are fungi and bacteria** (not viruses); common **mutualisms** include coral-zooxanthellae and lichen (fungus + alga), and protozoa living symbiotically in the guts of termites, helping digest wood; and a classification trap: the **sea cow and sea lion are mammals**, but the **sea horse is a fish**.

**Picture it**

| Phenomenon | Cause |
|---|---|
| Acid rain | SO2 + NOx |
| Photochemical smog | NOx + VOCs + sunlight (gives O3, PAN) |
| Eutrophication | Nutrient (N, P) enrichment of water |

**Terms explained**
- **SRM** = solar radiation management, reflecting sunlight to cool the planet.
- **VOC** = volatile organic compound (e.g. benzene).
- **Endocrine disruptor** = a chemical that interferes with hormones.
- **Decomposer** = an organism (fungi, bacteria) that breaks down dead matter.

**Don't confuse**
- **Natural nanoparticles DO exist** (soot, volcanic ash) — "only human-made" is false.
- **Excess N fertiliser suppresses, not multiplies, N-fixing microbes.**
- **Sea horse is a fish**, not a mammal.

**Remember it**
"Acid rain = S + N; smog = N + VOC + sun; sea horse = fish." BPA = polycarbonate.

**TL;DR**
- SRM (sulphate aerosols, cirrus thinning) aims to reduce warming; carbon fertilization = CO2-driven plant growth.
- Remote sensing measures chlorophyll, paddy GHGs, land-surface temperature; neem-coated urea slows urea release.
- Acid rain = SO2 + NOx; photochemical smog = NOx + VOC + sunlight (O3, PAN); excess N fertiliser acidifies soil and leaches nitrate.
- Decomposers are fungi/bacteria; sea cow and sea lion are mammals, sea horse is a fish; BPA is an endocrine disruptor.
keyPoints: Sulphate-aerosol injection and cirrus-cloud thinning are geoengineering methods to reduce global warming.
Carbon fertilization = higher plant growth due to increased atmospheric CO2.
Remote sensing can measure chlorophyll, paddy GHG emissions and land-surface temperature.
Neem-coated urea slows urea dissolution in soil, improving nitrogen-use efficiency.
Acid rain is caused by SO2 and NOx; photochemical smog needs NOx + VOCs + sunlight, forming O3 and PAN.
Excess nitrogenous fertilizer increases soil acidity and leaches nitrate to groundwater.
BPA is a component of polycarbonate plastic and an endocrine disruptor; benzene is a VOC from exhaust/tobacco/wood.
Decomposers are fungi and bacteria (not viruses); sea cow and sea lion are mammals while sea horse is a fish.

items.title: Global Environmental Conventions & the COP Timeline (Stockholm 1972 → COP31 Antalya 2026)
items.body:
## Every treaty, with its year, place and job

**In one line:** global environmental law grew from the Stockholm Conference (1972) and the Rio Earth Summit (1992) into a family of treaties — ozone (Vienna, Montreal, Kigali), chemicals (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata), land (UNCCD), biodiversity (CBD, Kunming–Montreal) and climate (UNFCCC, Kyoto, Paris) — with the climate COPs meeting every year, the next being COP31 at Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026.

**Why it is asked:** the Mains syllabus (M5-6) names **Montreal, Kyoto, CITES and COP21**; Prelims asks "Kigali Amendment controls", "Basel deals with", "Minamata is about", "30x30 target", "which COP set the $300 billion goal" and "India hosted which COP".

**The story**

The **Stockholm Conference (1972)** created **UNEP** and gave us **World Environment Day (5 June)**. The **Brundtland Report, "Our Common Future" (1987)**, defined **sustainable development** as meeting present needs without compromising future generations. The **Rio Earth Summit (1992)** produced **Agenda 21**, the **UNFCCC**, the **CBD** and the path to the **UNCCD (1994)** on desertification. The **ozone** regime is the most successful: the **Vienna Convention (1985)** and **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phase out CFCs, and the **Kigali Amendment (2016)** phases down **HFCs** (powerful greenhouse gases). Chemicals are covered by **Basel (1989, hazardous-waste movement)**, **Rotterdam (1998, prior informed consent)**, **Stockholm (2001, persistent organic pollutants)** and **Minamata (2013, mercury)**.

For nature, the **Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (CBD COP15, December 2022)** set **23 targets**, including **"30x30"** — protecting **30% of land and sea by 2030**. The **High Seas (BBNJ) Treaty** on marine life beyond national waters entered into force in **January 2026**. For climate, COPs run yearly: **COP3 Kyoto (1997)**, **COP8 New Delhi (2002, hosted by India)**, **COP15 Copenhagen (2009)**, **COP21 Paris (2015)**, **COP26 Glasgow (2021)**, **COP29 Baku (2024)** — which set a **new climate-finance goal of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035** — and **COP30 Belém (2025)**. **COP31** is being held at **Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November 2026)**, with **Australia presiding over the negotiations** under a compromise struck at Belém.

### Conventions and protocols

| Instrument | Year and focus |
|---|---|
| **Stockholm Conference** | 1972 — created UNEP; World Environment Day 5 June |
| **Brundtland Report ("Our Common Future")** | 1987 — defined sustainable development |
| **Rio Earth Summit** | 1992 — Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD |
| **Vienna Convention** | 1985 — framework for protecting the ozone layer |
| **Montreal Protocol** | 1987 — phases out ozone-depleting CFCs; the first treaty ratified by every UN member |
| **Kigali Amendment** | 2016 — phases down HFCs; India by 85% between 2032 and 2047 |
| **Basel Convention** | 1989 — transboundary movement of hazardous wastes |
| **Rotterdam Convention** | 1998 — prior informed consent for trade in hazardous chemicals |
| **Stockholm Convention** | 2001 — persistent organic pollutants (POPs) such as DDT |
| **Minamata Convention** | 2013 — mercury pollution |
| **UNCCD** | 1994 — desertification; India hosted COP14 at Greater Noida (2019) |
| **Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework** | CBD COP15, December 2022 — 23 targets incl. 30x30 (protect 30% of land and sea by 2030) |
| **CBD COP16 (Cali, Colombia, 2024)** | set up the Cali Fund for benefits from digital sequence information |
| **High Seas (BBNJ) Treaty** | adopted 2023; entered into force January 2026 — marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction |
| **International Whaling Commission** | 1946 — moratorium on commercial whaling since 1986 |

### Climate COP timeline

| COP | Outcome |
|---|---|
| **COP1 (Berlin, 1995)** | first Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC |
| **COP3 (Kyoto, 1997)** | Kyoto Protocol — binding cuts for developed countries; CDM carbon credits |
| **COP8 (New Delhi, 2002)** | the climate COP hosted by India — Delhi Declaration |
| **COP15 (Copenhagen, 2009)** | Copenhagen Accord — US$100 billion a year climate-finance pledge |
| **COP16 (Cancún, 2010)** | set up the Green Climate Fund |
| **COP21 (Paris, 2015)** | Paris Agreement; International Solar Alliance launched |
| **COP26 (Glasgow, 2021)** | Glasgow Climate Pact — coal 'phase down'; India's Panchamrit |
| **COP29 (Baku, 2024)** | New Collective Quantified Goal — at least US$300 billion a year by 2035; Article 6 carbon-market rules |
| **COP30 (Belém, November 2025)** | held in the Amazon; launched the Tropical Forest Forever Facility |
| **COP31 (Antalya, Türkiye, 9–20 November 2026)** | hosted by Türkiye with Australia presiding over the negotiations |

## Don't confuse
- **Stockholm Conference (1972) = UNEP; Stockholm Convention (2001) = POPs.**
- **Montreal (1987) = CFCs (ozone); Kigali (2016) = HFCs (climate); Kyoto (1997) = GHG cuts.**
- **Basel = hazardous waste; Rotterdam = prior informed consent; Minamata = mercury.**
- **Kunming–Montreal 30x30 is a CBD target**, not a climate (UNFCCC) target.
- **COP30 = Belém, Brazil (2025); COP31 = Antalya, Türkiye (2026).** India hosted climate **COP8 (2002)** and desertification **COP14 (2019)**.

**Remember it:** "BRSM for chemicals — Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Minamata."

**TL;DR**
- Stockholm 1972 (UNEP) → Brundtland 1987 → Rio 1992 (UNFCCC, CBD, Agenda 21) → UNCCD 1994.
- Ozone: Vienna 1985, Montreal 1987, Kigali 2016 (HFCs). Chemicals: Basel 1989, Rotterdam 1998, Stockholm 2001, Minamata 2013.
- Nature: Kunming–Montreal GBF 2022 (30x30), Cali Fund 2024, BBNJ in force 2026.
- COPs: Kyoto 1997, New Delhi 2002, Copenhagen 2009, Paris 2015, Glasgow 2021, Baku 2024 ($300 bn), Belém 2025, Antalya 2026.
keyPoints: Stockholm Conference — 1972 — created UNEP; World Environment Day 5 June.
Brundtland Report ("Our Common Future") — 1987 — defined sustainable development.
COP3 (Kyoto, 1997) — Kyoto Protocol — binding cuts for developed countries; CDM carbon credits.
COP8 (New Delhi, 2002) — the climate COP hosted by India — Delhi Declaration.

items.title: Pollution Science, Waste Rules & Green Schemes
items.body:
## How pollution works, and the rules that fight it

**In one line:** pollution science comes down to a few measures (PM2.5, AQI, BOD, dissolved oxygen), a few processes (ozone depletion, biomagnification, eutrophication) and a few disasters (Minamata, Itai-itai, Bhopal); India answers with waste-management rules and green schemes.

**Why it is asked:** "high BOD means", "biomagnification of DDT", "Minamata disease is caused by", "blue-baby syndrome", "the gas at Bhopal", "plastic carry-bag thickness", "bio-medical waste colour codes", "Green Credit Programme" and "MISHTI is for" are frequent items (syllabus M5-6: pollution and solid-waste management).

**The story**

Air quality is reported as **PM2.5 and PM10** (particles smaller than 2.5 and 10 micrometres) and combined into the **AQI**; in Delhi-NCR, the **Commission for Air Quality Management (2021)** enforces the **Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)**. In water, **BOD (biochemical oxygen demand)** is the oxygen microbes need to break down organic waste — **high BOD means more pollution** and less **dissolved oxygen** for fish. Too many nutrients cause **eutrophication** and algal blooms. Some poisons build up along food chains (**biomagnification**): **DDT** thinned the eggshells of birds, **mercury** caused **Minamata disease** in Japan and **cadmium** caused **Itai-itai**. **Nitrate** in drinking water causes **blue-baby syndrome**; **arsenic** in groundwater affects West Bengal and Bihar. The ozone layer in the **stratosphere** is measured in **Dobson units**; CFCs opened the **Antarctic ozone hole** — but ozone at **ground level** is a pollutant. The **Bhopal gas tragedy (2–3 December 1984)** released **methyl isocyanate (MIC)**.

India's waste rules (all under the EP Act 1986) cover **solid waste, plastics, e-waste, batteries and bio-medical waste**, built on **Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)** — makers must collect back what they sell.

### Pollution science

| Term | Meaning / fact |
|---|---|
| **PM2.5** | fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres — reach deep into the lungs |
| **GRAP** | Graded Response Action Plan for Delhi-NCR, enforced by the Commission for Air Quality Management (2021) |
| **BOD (biochemical oxygen demand)** | oxygen needed by microbes to break down organic waste — high BOD = more polluted water |
| **Dissolved oxygen (DO)** | falls as pollution rises; fish die when it is too low |
| **Biomagnification** | rise in concentration of a poison (e.g. DDT) at each higher trophic level |
| **Minamata disease** | mercury poisoning from contaminated fish (Japan) |
| **Itai-itai disease** | cadmium poisoning (Japan) — painful bones |
| **Blue-baby syndrome** | nitrate in drinking water reduces oxygen in infants' blood |
| **Arsenic poisoning** | arsenic-rich groundwater in West Bengal and Bihar |
| **Dobson unit** | unit for measuring ozone in the atmosphere |
| **Ozone hole** | CFC-driven thinning of stratospheric ozone, worst over Antarctica |
| **Ground-level ozone** | a harmful pollutant formed in photochemical smog (good up high, bad nearby) |
| **Bhopal gas tragedy (2–3 December 1984)** | leak of methyl isocyanate (MIC) from the Union Carbide plant |
| **Algal bloom** | explosive algae growth from excess N and P (eutrophication), causing "dead zones" |

### Waste rules and green schemes

| Rule / scheme | Key feature |
|---|---|
| **Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016** | segregation at source into wet, dry and hazardous waste |
| **Plastic Waste Management Rules (amended 2021–22)** | carry bags must be at least 120 microns (from December 2022); EPR for producers |
| **E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022** | producers meet EPR recycling targets through registered recyclers |
| **Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022** | EPR for all battery types, including EV batteries |
| **Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016** | colour-coded bags: yellow, red, white (translucent) and blue |
| **CRZ Notification, 2019** | Coastal Regulation Zone — limits building near the high-tide line |
| **EIA Notification, 2006** | Environmental Impact Assessment required before clearing listed projects |
| **Green Credit Programme (October 2023)** | market-based credits for actions such as tree planting and water conservation |
| **Namami Gange (2014)** | integrated mission to clean and conserve the Ganga |
| **MISHTI (2023)** | Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes — mangrove planting |
| **Amrit Dharohar (2023)** | scheme to conserve Ramsar wetlands and promote eco-tourism |
| **Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam (June 2024)** | tree-planting campaign launched on World Environment Day |
| **Green India Mission** | NAPCC mission to increase forest and tree cover |
| **National Green Tribunal** | principal bench New Delhi; zonal benches Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata, Chennai |

## Don't confuse
- **High BOD = dirty water; high DO = clean water.**
- **Minamata = mercury; Itai-itai = cadmium; blue baby = nitrate; Bhopal = methyl isocyanate.**
- **Stratospheric ozone protects us; ground-level ozone is a pollutant.**
- **Green Credit Programme** (environmental actions) ≠ **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme** (emissions market).

**Remember it:** "Mercury–Minamata, Cadmium–Itai-itai, Nitrate–blue baby."

**TL;DR**
- PM2.5, AQI, GRAP (CAQM 2021); BOD high = polluted; DO low = fish die.
- Biomagnification (DDT); Minamata (mercury), Itai-itai (cadmium), blue baby (nitrate), arsenic (West Bengal).
- Ozone: Dobson units; Antarctic hole; ground ozone is a pollutant. Bhopal 1984 = MIC.
- Rules: SWM 2016, plastic 120 microns, e-waste and battery rules 2022, BMW 2016, CRZ 2019, EIA 2006.
- Schemes: Green Credit Programme, Namami Gange, MISHTI, Amrit Dharohar, Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam.
keyPoints: PM2.5 — fine particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres — reach deep into the lungs.
GRAP — Graded Response Action Plan for Delhi-NCR, enforced by the Commission for Air Quality Management (2021).
Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 — segregation at source into wet, dry and hazardous waste.
Plastic Waste Management Rules (amended 2021–22) — carry bags must be at least 120 microns (from December 2022); EPR for producers.

items.title: Threatened Species, Wildlife Censuses & Species Projects
items.body:
## Which animal, which status, which project

**In one line:** the IUCN Red List ranks species from Least Concern to Extinct, India's flagship species each have a project and a census figure, and examiners pair species with their status, state or protected area.

**Why it is asked:** "IUCN headquarters", "which of these is Critically Endangered", "national aquatic animal", "latest lion/elephant/snow-leopard count", "diclofenac and vultures" and "Project Crocodile began at" are frequent items.

**The story**

The **IUCN (1948, HQ Gland, Switzerland)** publishes the **Red List**: from safest to gone — **Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct**. India's **Critically Endangered** list includes the **Great Indian Bustard**, the **gharial**, **Jerdon's courser** (rediscovered in **1986** in Andhra Pradesh) and the **white-rumped vulture**, whose numbers crashed because of the cattle painkiller **diclofenac** (banned for veterinary use in **2006**). The **Ganges river dolphin** became India's **national aquatic animal (2009)** and the **elephant** its **national heritage animal (2010)**; the **tiger** has been the national animal since **1973**.

Census figures examiners use: **3,682 tigers (2022)** — about 70% of the world's; **891 Asiatic lions (2025, Gir landscape, Gujarat)**; **22,446 elephants** in the first **DNA-based count (2025)**; and **718 snow leopards** (first national estimate, **2024**). The cheetah was declared **extinct in India in 1952** before Project Cheetah (2022).

### IUCN and threatened species

| Species / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **IUCN** | founded 1948, HQ Gland, Switzerland — publishes the Red List |
| **Red List categories (safest → gone)** | Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct |
| **Great Indian Bustard** | Critically Endangered — Desert NP (Rajasthan); historically Rollapadu (AP); power lines a key threat |
| **Gharial** | Critically Endangered fish-eating crocodile — National Chambal Sanctuary |
| **Jerdon's courser** | Critically Endangered bird rediscovered in 1986 near Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa, AP) |
| **Vultures and diclofenac** | veterinary diclofenac caused a crash; banned for animals in 2006 |
| **Ganges river dolphin** | national aquatic animal (2009); Endangered; Project Dolphin |
| **Elephant** | declared national heritage animal in 2010 |
| **One-horned rhinoceros** | Vulnerable; most live in Kaziranga NP (Assam) |
| **Asiatic lion** | only wild population in the Gir landscape, Gujarat — 891 in 2025 |
| **Elephant count (2025)** | 22,446 — first DNA-based all-India estimate |
| **Snow leopard** | 718 in India (first national estimate, 2024); Vulnerable |
| **Cheetah** | declared extinct in India in 1952 |
| **Hangul (Kashmir stag)** | Kashmir red deer found mainly in Dachigam NP (J&K) |
| **Sangai (brow-antlered deer)** | lives only on the floating Keibul Lamjao NP, Loktak Lake (Manipur) |
| **Lion-tailed macaque** | endemic primate of the Western Ghats — Silent Valley |

### Species projects

| Project | Year / fact |
|---|---|
| **Project Crocodile** | 1975 — began at Bhitarkanika (Odisha) |
| **Project Snow Leopard** | 2009 — high-altitude Himalayan conservation |
| **Project Dolphin** | announced 2020 — river and marine dolphins |
| **Project Tiger start** | 1973 with nine tiger reserves (first: Jim Corbett) |
| **58th tiger reserve** | Madhav (Madhya Pradesh), March 2025 |
| **GIB conservation breeding** | Jaisalmer centre (Rajasthan) under the Great Indian Bustard programme |

## Don't confuse
- **Critically Endangered (CR) is worse than Endangered (EN), which is worse than Vulnerable (VU).**
- **National animal = tiger; national aquatic animal = Ganges river dolphin; national heritage animal = elephant.**
- **Hangul = Dachigam; sangai = Keibul Lamjao (Loktak); lion-tailed macaque = Silent Valley.**
- **Jerdon's courser** is an AP bird (Sri Lankamalleswara) — not the Great Indian Bustard.

**Remember it:** "LC-NT-VU-EN-CR-EW-EX: from Least Concern to Extinct."

**TL;DR**
- IUCN (1948, Gland); Red List order LC → NT → VU → EN → CR → EW → EX.
- CR: GIB, gharial, Jerdon's courser (AP), white-rumped vulture (diclofenac banned 2006); hangul lives in Dachigam.
- Counts: tigers 3,682 (2022), lions 891 (2025), elephants 22,446 (DNA, 2025), snow leopards 718 (2024); cheetah extinct 1952.
- Projects: Tiger 1973, Crocodile 1975, Elephant 1992, Snow Leopard 2009, Dolphin 2020, Cheetah 2022.
keyPoints: IUCN — founded 1948, HQ Gland, Switzerland — publishes the Red List.
Red List categories (safest → gone) — Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild, Extinct.
Project Crocodile — 1975 — began at Bhitarkanika (Odisha).

items.title: National Parks, Natural Heritage Sites, Ecology Hotspots of India & Green Movements
items.body:
## The famous parks, the UNESCO sites and the people's movements

**In one line:** India's first national park is Jim Corbett (1936), its largest is Hemis (Ladakh), its natural World Heritage Sites run from Kaziranga to the Western Ghats, and its green movements — Bishnoi, Chipko, Appiko, Silent Valley, Narmada Bachao — are favourite history-of-environment questions.

**Why it is asked:** "first national park", "floating national park", "Gadgil vs Kasturirangan", "Chipko was led by", "Khejarli sacrifice" and "which natural site is on the UNESCO list" are steady Prelims items; the Western Ghats debate is Mains material.

**The story**

**Jim Corbett National Park (1936, first as Hailey National Park)** in Uttarakhand was India's first; **Hemis (Ladakh)** is the largest. **Keoladeo (Bharatpur)**, once the winter home of the Siberian crane, and **Chilika** were India's **first two Ramsar sites (1981)**; the **Sundarbans** is the **largest Ramsar site**. India's coral reefs are in the **Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands**. For the **Western Ghats**, the **Gadgil panel (2011)** wanted about **64%** of the range treated as ecologically sensitive, while the **Kasturirangan panel (2013)** proposed about **37%**.

People defended forests long before the laws: in **1730 Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois** died at **Khejarli (Rajasthan)** protecting khejri trees; the **Chipko movement (1973, Uttarakhand)** — Gaura Devi, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt — hugged trees; **Appiko (1983)** copied it in Karnataka; the **Silent Valley** campaign (Kerala) stopped a dam; and **Narmada Bachao Andolan (Medha Patkar)** opposed big dams.

### Parks, sites and ecology facts

| Place | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Jim Corbett NP (Uttarakhand)** | India's first national park — 1936, as Hailey National Park |
| **Hemis NP (Ladakh)** | India's largest national park — snow leopards |
| **Keibul Lamjao NP (Manipur)** | the world's only floating national park, on Loktak Lake |
| **Gir NP (Gujarat)** | only home of the Asiatic lion |
| **First Indian Ramsar sites** | Chilika (Odisha) and Keoladeo (Rajasthan), 1 October 1981 |
| **Largest Ramsar site in India** | Sundarban Wetland, West Bengal (about 4,230 km²) |
| **Natural World Heritage Sites** | Kaziranga, Keoladeo, Manas, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi & Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats, Great Himalayan NP; Khangchendzonga (mixed) |
| **Coral reefs of India** | Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar |
| **Gadgil (WGEEP, 2011) vs Kasturirangan (2013)** | about 64% vs about 37% of the Western Ghats as ecologically sensitive |
| **Eco-Sensitive Zone** | buffer of up to 10 km around a protected area by default |
| **Mangroves (ISFR 2023)** | West Bengal has the most, then Gujarat |

### Environmental movements

| Movement | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Khejarli sacrifice (1730)** | Amrita Devi and 363 Bishnois died protecting khejri trees (Rajasthan) |
| **Chipko (1973)** | tree-hugging movement in Uttarakhand — Gaura Devi, Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt |
| **Appiko (1983)** | Karnataka's version of Chipko — Panduranga Hegde |
| **Save Silent Valley** | Kerala campaign that stopped a hydro dam; Silent Valley became a NP (1984) |
| **Narmada Bachao Andolan** | Medha Patkar and Baba Amte against large Narmada dams (Sardar Sarovar) |
| **Jungle Bachao Andolan** | tribal movement in Jharkhand (then Bihar) against teak plantations replacing sal |

## Don't confuse
- **First NP = Jim Corbett (1936); largest NP = Hemis; largest tiger reserve = Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (AP).**
- **First Ramsar sites = Chilika and Keoladeo (1981); largest Ramsar site = Sundarban.**
- **Gadgil = about 64% sensitive; Kasturirangan = about 37%.**
- **Chipko = Uttarakhand (1973); Appiko = Karnataka (1983); Khejarli = Rajasthan (1730).**

**Remember it:** "Chipko hugged, Appiko copied, Bishnois gave their lives first."

**TL;DR**
- Corbett 1936 (first NP); Hemis largest; Keibul Lamjao floating; Gir = Asiatic lion.
- First Ramsar sites Chilika and Keoladeo (1981); Sundarban largest; coral reefs at Mannar, Kutch, Lakshadweep, A&N.
- Western Ghats: Gadgil 2011 (~64%) vs Kasturirangan 2013 (~37%); ESZ up to 10 km.
- Movements: Khejarli 1730, Chipko 1973, Appiko 1983, Silent Valley, Narmada Bachao.

Hemis NP (Ladakh) — India's largest national park — snow leopards.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Environment — More Sites, Species, State Symbols & Forest Data
items.body:
## The rest of AP's environment map

**In one line:** beyond Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam, Coringa, Kolleru and Pulicat, Andhra Pradesh has sanctuaries for the blackbuck, the Jerdon's courser and pelicans, official state symbols (blackbuck, rose-ringed parakeet, neem, jasmine), and about 18% forest cover.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC likes "AP's state animal/bird", "Nelapattu is known for", "Sri Lankamalleswara protects", "AP's forest cover per ISFR 2023", "Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary is a mangrove area" and the latest national Ramsar count.

**The story**

In **2018 Andhra Pradesh** adopted the **blackbuck** as its **state animal**, the **rose-ringed parakeet** as its **state bird**, the **neem** as its **state tree** and **jasmine** as its **state flower**. **Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary** (Tirupati district, near Pulicat) is a major breeding site of the **spot-billed pelican**. **Sri Lankamalleswara WLS** (Kadapa) shelters the **Jerdon's courser**. The **Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary**, in the Krishna estuary, is AP's second mangrove sanctuary after Coringa. **Kambalakonda** (Visakhapatnam) protects Eastern Ghats forest near the city. As per **ISFR 2023**, AP's **forest cover is about 29,784 km², or about 18.3%** of its area — below the national 21.76%.

Nationally, India had **103 Ramsar sites by October 2026**; two more — **Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh) and Sukhna Lake (Chandigarh)** — were reported on **15 October 2026**, taking the count to **103**. Kolleru is still AP's only Ramsar site.

### Andhra Pradesh sites, species and symbols

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **AP state symbols (2018)** | animal blackbuck; bird rose-ringed parakeet; tree neem; flower jasmine |
| **Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary** | breeding site of the spot-billed pelican, near Pulicat |
| **Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa)** | habitat of the Critically Endangered Jerdon's courser |
| **Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary** | mangrove sanctuary in the Krishna estuary |
| **Kambalakonda WLS** | Eastern Ghats forest sanctuary at Visakhapatnam |
| **AP forest cover (ISFR 2023)** | about 29,784 km² — about 18.3% of the state, below the national 21.76% |
| **Nallamala hills** | Eastern Ghats range holding the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve and red sanders |
| **Ramsar sites reported on 15 October 2026** | Sauj Jheel (UP) and Sukhna Lake (Chandigarh) — 102nd and 103rd |
| **Olive Ridley on the AP coast** | nests on AP beaches such as those of Srikakulam and Visakhapatnam |

## Don't confuse
- **AP state animal = blackbuck** (not the tiger); **state bird = rose-ringed parakeet** (the Indian roller was the old symbol of undivided AP).
- **Nelapattu = pelicans; Sri Lankamalleswara = Jerdon's courser; Rollapadu = Great Indian Bustard.**
- **Coringa (Godavari) and Krishna WLS (Krishna)** are AP's two mangrove sanctuaries.
- **Ramsar count:** 101 (August 2026) → 103 reported (15 October 2026). AP still has one (Kolleru).

**Remember it:** "Buck, parrot, neem, jasmine — AP's four symbols."

**TL;DR**
- AP symbols (2018): blackbuck, rose-ringed parakeet, neem, jasmine.
- Nelapattu (pelicans), Sri Lankamalleswara (Jerdon's courser), Krishna WLS (mangroves), Kambalakonda (Vizag).
- AP forest cover about 18.3% (ISFR 2023) vs India 21.76%.
- India's Ramsar sites: 101 (Aug 2026), 103 reported on 15 Oct 2026.
keyPoints: AP state symbols (2018) — animal blackbuck; bird rose-ringed parakeet; tree neem; flower jasmine.
Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary — breeding site of the spot-billed pelican, near Pulicat.

items.title: For Mains — Environment, Biodiversity & Climate Change
items.body:
### For Mains — Environment, biodiversity and climate change

**In one line**
For Paper-5, argue the development-versus-environment balance using India's climate pledges, conservation framework and nature-based coastal resilience.

**Why it is asked**
The syllabus clauses cover "development vs environment; pollution; climate change; natural disasters" and "environmental legislation (Montreal/Kyoto/CITES/COP21); SDGs", so answers must weigh growth against sustainability.

**The story**
Mains questions ask you to **evaluate and prescribe** — India's climate commitments, biodiversity-conservation gaps, or wetland and disaster resilience. Build around dimensions and quote dated instruments.

**Picture it**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Problem | Climate change, pollution, biodiversity loss, disasters |
| Commitments | Panchamrit (COP26), net-zero 2070, NDCs, SDGs |
| Framework | EPA 1986, WPA 1972, Forest Act (2023), NAPCC's 8 missions, NGT |
| Conventions | UNFCCC/Kyoto/Paris, CBD/Cartagena/Nagoya, Ramsar, CITES |
| Limitations | Forest diversion, man-animal conflict, finance gaps, enforcement |
| Way forward | Nature-based solutions, CAMPA funding, community participation, One Health |

**Facts to quote**
- Panchamrit: **500 GW** non-fossil, net-zero **2070**; India leads **ISA** and **CDRI**.
- **103 Ramsar sites (2026)**; **58 tiger reserves**; ISFR 2023 forest+tree cover **25.17%**.
- **COP30 (Belem, Nov 2025)**; Loss and Damage Fund (COP27, 2022).
- AP angle: **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam** (largest tiger reserve), **Coringa** mangroves (AP had the largest mangrove increase in ISFR 2023), **Kolleru** Ramsar site, cyclone resilience under the **DM Act 2005 / Sendai**.

**Terms explained**
- **Blue carbon** = carbon captured by coastal ecosystems like mangroves.
- **Nature-based solution** = using ecosystems (mangroves, wetlands) to solve problems like flooding.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite mangrove bio-shields and the 1999 Odisha super-cyclone for disaster resilience.
- Quote: India's "net-zero by 2070" pledge to frame climate ambition versus equity.
- Diagram idea: a see-saw balancing "development" against "environment", stabilised by sustainability.

**TL;DR**
- Frame as development vs environment, backed by SDGs and net-zero 2070.
- Anchor with EPA 1986, NAPCC's 8 missions, Paris Agreement and Ramsar/CITES.
- Quote 103 Ramsar sites, 58 tiger reserves, ISFR 2023, COP30 Belem 2025.
- Bring the AP angle: NSTR, Coringa mangroves, Kolleru, cyclone resilience.
keyPoints: Mains (Paper-5) asks you to balance development vs environment, backed by SDGs and net-zero 2070.
Climate: Panchamrit (COP26) — 500 GW non-fossil, net-zero 2070; India leads ISA and CDRI; COP30 at Belem (2025).
Framework to quote: EPA 1986, WPA 1972, Forest Act (renamed 2023), NAPCC's 8 missions, NGT 2010.
Conservation data: 103 Ramsar sites (2026), 58 tiger reserves, ISFR 2023 forest+tree cover 25.17%.
AP angle: Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (largest tiger reserve), Coringa mangroves, Kolleru Ramsar site, cyclone resilience (DM Act 2005, Sendai).
Way forward: nature-based solutions, CAMPA funding, community participation and One Health.
